title: "When the Shit Hits"

subtitle: "In Memory of Yee"

Spring 2017\. Facebook’s new rooftop garden. Succulents lined the planters like tidy little fists.  Near the corner, a little booth was setting up a ginger-shot station—tiny plastic cups, a blender whining, that sharp smell catching in your throat. Beneath the decking, ad auctions churned along—money moving invisibly under our feet.

I was sick then, though nobody could tell me why. It wasn’t dramatic. It was worse: it was consistent. Every afternoon, right on schedule, a heavy fatigue hit me out of nowhere, as if someone reached in and turned the brightness down on my body. The tests all came back “normal,” a word that makes you feel briefly relieved and then quietly insane.

Yee noticed—not with a dramatic “Are you okay?” in front of people, but with the quiet accuracy of someone paying attention. He caught my voice thinning late in the day, and how I kept moving afternoon meetings to the morning.

So I told him. 

He didn’t do the thing people do now—where you say, “Let me know how I can help,” and then fade back into meetings. Many times, he’d steer us to a bench in the rooftop garden, under a patch of shade. He’d set his paper cup down, angle his knees toward me, and check in—quiet, steady, unshowy. Once he said, almost offhand, “Hey, I asked around.” A couple clinics nearby. “This person helped my friend,” he said. “And this other one is annoyingly thorough.” He wrote the addresses on the back of a receipt. He didn’t text it. He wrote it—like paper made things real.

At some point I asked him the question a sick person tired of day-to-day work asks when they’re trying to make sense of the future. I asked it not out of curiosity, but out of fear.

“What would you do after retiring?” I asked.

Without missing a beat, he said: “*Writing*.” 

The word landed wrong at first, like I’d misheard him. I waited for the grin, the follow-up, the wink that would turn it into a joke. There wasn’t one. 

And that surprised me.

Yee always felt kinetic. Like a man whose default mode was “light cardio,” even when he was standing still. His laugh came easy—bright, with momentum. He shaved his head once a year like he was renewing a subscription; you could hear the buzz, see the reset. In the office he’d challenge me to do pushups on the floor surrounded by standup desks, like humiliation was a wellness program. On a business trip in London, he invited me to do a sprint on the street—not in a park, not on a track, but just on the street—casually, like we were auditioning for a sneaker commercial. 

So hearing “*writing*” felt like spotting a secret door in a building you thought you knew. A door he’d been carrying around quietly, while the rest of us watched him run.

*Writing,* I thought. Huh. I filed it away the way you file away small, strange facts about people you like. And then life kept moving. The machine kept humming.

![][image1]  
Yee and I sat at the far end of the table during a Facebook team lunch.

A few months ago, I got the news on Facebook—where everything important arrives wearing the same clothes as everything else. Someone’s vacation. Someone’s engagement. An ad for socks. And then, in the same scroll, his family wrote: 

“Yee passed away peacefully in his sleep on September 21st.”

Below the text was a photo—Yee stretched out on a sun-warmed slab of granite beside a lake, one arm behind his head, the sky huge and clean above him. It looked like rest. It looked like a vacation. So calm it looked like a mistake. No clear villain. No neat ending. Just… gone.

I didn’t respond to the post. I hovered a thumb over the heart reaction and it felt insulting. I typed *What the hell* into the comment box and deleted it. 

I couldn’t picture Yee “peacefully in his sleep.” It didn’t compute. The brain has a model of the people in your life—who they are, what happens next—and Yee’s model didn’t include “dies quietly of something without a name.” Quiet deaths belonged to quiet men. Yee was the guy who would outlive the rest of us out of spite and lung capacity. 

And then grief did what it always does when it can’t carry the big story: it shrank it into smaller scenes. Little clips. A highlight reel of who someone was to you.

Here’s one of mine.

In the summer of 2017, my doctor, at his wits’ end, talked me into sinus surgery after spotting polyps, like a few speed bumps in the sinus plumbing could explain years of fatigue. The night before, I went in for a last round of pre-op labs. He gave me the usual bargain: “If something’s wrong, I’ll call tonight. Otherwise, be here at 7:30 a.m.” So when the phone rang at 2:00 a.m., I thought: That’s it. Surgery’s off. Bad news.

Instead, a young colleague’s voice came through, small and shaken: “I’m in jail.”

He’d immigrated from China with his wife and their one-year-old a few months earlier. New apartment. New job. New country. Not much money in the bank account. From the outside it looked clean. It wasn’t.

His wife was suffering in the long shadow that sometimes follows childbirth, when the mind becomes an unrecognizable room and you’re locked inside it. That night, they argued. The police were called. And in the way these stories go—fast, brutal, absurd—he was taken away.

Then the line went dead—cut short by whatever rules govern those phones—before he could tell me where he was.

There are few sensations like that: being handed responsibility with no coordinates. I didn’t even know his home address—where he’d been arrested. I only knew, vaguely, that he lived somewhere in the South Bay, that wide sprawl of jurisdictions where a person can vanish into the seams.

Before dawn, I called Yee. I told him what I had, which was almost nothing.

We could’ve gone to HR. We could’ve thrown the whole thing into the company’s hands, let Facebook “handle it,” even just to find his address.

Yee didn’t want that. Not even for something as basic as where the guy lived.

He said it plainly: we didn’t know what the system would do to him. Not just the legal system—the corporate one. His job. His record. His immigration status. A domestic incident can metastasize fast when you’re new to a country and everything you’ve built is still wet cement. Yee didn’t want to add more machinery to the problem. He wanted fewer people, fewer files, fewer irreversible steps.

“Go to the hospital,” he said. “I’ll take care of it.”

In the early afternoon when I came out of anesthesia, my doctor—who had the bedside manner of an airline safety video—told me: “Don’t make any big decisions today.”

I couldn’t form a coherent sentence. My mind still didn’t have control of my body. 

I called Yee.

He didn’t narrate what he’d done. He didn’t dramatize it. He just said: “I found him.”

He never told me how many numbers he dialed, how many times he got transferred, how many dead ends he swallowed and tried again—never then, not even later over beer and laughter. All I knew was the outcome: after six hours of doing the unglamorous work, he’d found the jail. He’d spoken to the police. He’d pulled a clean, usable fact out of the maze.

Bail: $10,000.

We decided to chip in to bail him out. Fuck the “no big decision today.” 

So I sent my wife to withdraw $5,000 from the bank, and then meet Yee in a grocery store parking lot close to our house. I stayed behind—post-surgery, half-awake—while my wife did something that still sounds fake when I say it out loud.

“How does he look?” my wife asked me.

I said, “Big guy. Always in a black shirt. Might wear black sunglasses.”

She paused. “So… like a gangster?”

Yes. Exactly.

Later she told me what it looked like. Yee just walked up—big guy, black shirt, exactly as described. Not threatening, but capable. 

“The first thing he asked,” my wife said, “was how you were doing.”

She told him: “He’s okay. But he can’t really move: He would faint.”

Yee nodded, like he filed that information somewhere safe. He looked at the envelope, tucked it away, and said something like he was checking items off a list.

“Alright,” he said. “One piece of shit at a time.”

It was absurd and true and somehow exactly what you needed to hear in a grocery store parking lot while holding five thousand dollars in cash. Your husband is one shit, he seemed to be saying. This is another.

That was Yee.

He wasn’t the loud hero. He was just there, doing the work, making the calls, solving the problem in front of him.

Which I’d later realize was exactly what his writing was: turning panic into a next step.

Years passed. I left Facebook. Yee stayed. We didn’t keep close contact—the way people often don’t, even when they like each other, because adulthood is an endless conveyor belt of logistics and laundry. I did call Yee when my doctor finally diagnosed my problem—it was sleep apnea, and my brain was waking up 56 times every hour to restart breathing. The sinus surgery was totally meaningless. Yee congratulated me; we laughed, but my real recovery didn’t come until after three years.

Then one day Yee called. We met at Blue Bottle on University Ave in Palo Alto.

Blue Bottle was doing its Blue Bottle thing. Around us: the Palo Alto ecosystem in its natural habitat. Men in vests and women in crisp sneakers leaning over laptops. Founders saying words like *runway* and *seed round*. Someone at the next table drawing a revenue funnel on a napkin. A podcast laugh. A handshake. The quiet choreography of people trying to become inevitable.

Yee chose a small table near the back entrance. His cup warmed his hands. He kept turning it a little, rotating the sleeve without noticing he was doing it.

He didn’t ease into it with “so…” or a preamble. He just told me.

His son had become his daughter.

The way he said it is what I remember. Not theatrical. It wasn’t framed as a problem to debate. It was framed as a fact to honor. His voice stayed level. He didn’t say the things many fathers say when their kid hands them their true self.

He used her name. He corrected himself once—quietly, without drama—and then got it right the next time. He mentioned small logistical things in passing, the kind that don’t stick in memory as facts but do stick as evidence: forms updated, calls made, appointments lined up, the mundane scaffolding that makes a life livable. It was love expressed in procedure. 

Then, almost seamlessly he shifted topics. 

He asked me about China. Not vaguely. Specifically. What it feels like to be a kid there. What elementary school is like: the classroom rhythm, the rules, the pressure. Whether teachers enforce conformity in the small daily ways—hair, uniforms, posture, the right kind of silence. Whether there’s room for a child to be different without it becoming a public trial. He asked about bullying, about how parents talk, about what “normal” means in the air. He asked about paperwork—hukou, enrollment, transfers—as if he was already mapping the constraints. He asked about language immersion, international schools, which cities breathe easier. 

I realized, sitting there with the espresso heat rising between us, that he wasn’t shopping for opinions. He was building an escape plan. A new start. A place where his daughter could walk into a classroom without feeling every eye land on her.

But at that moment, I didn’t really understand what Yee had been carrying. I answered like an analyst instead of a friend. I told him, matter-of-factly, that China’s education system is brutal, and it’s hard for kids to be themselves. I talked about pressure like it was weather. I told the truth, but without wrapping it in care. I can still see his face as he listened—calm, attentive, taking it in—not arguing, not flinching, just absorbing another hard constraint.

Later, I wished I’d done something different. I wished I’d paused—asked how *he* was holding up, offered something besides facts. But Yee wasn’t asking to be comforted. He was trying to move his kid to safer ground, and he kept doing what he always did: moving forward.

Eventually he and his family moved to Hawaii. On Facebook, it looked like the kind of decision people daydream about at their desks—the whole family on an endless vacation. But I’ve learned not to trust the postcard: it was more like a door closing softly behind them.

I also learned Yee joined a company working on planting trees, building technology for global reforestation. Crazy decision for someone who worked on Facebook search. But it fit him. He needed to fix actual physical reality—red dirt under boots, seedlings in trays, satellite maps turning green. 

That’s how I imagined.

The most recent time I heard from Yee, I heard from him on LinkedIn.

Yee said he’d start a newsletter.

*Writing\!*

I didn’t read it at the time. Busy life. The usual lie.

In the weeks after, my mind kept going blank. And then the word *writing* came back like a knock. So I searched. 

And what I found is this:

Yee is survived by a newsletter full of shit.

Literally. It’s called *The New New Shit*. Eighteen episodes, each one titled like a dare: *Medieval Shit. Modern Shit. Carbon Is The New Shit. Shitty Data. Your AI is Full of Shit.* At first it sounds like a joking provocation. Then you realize it’s a worldview—like what he said to my wife, “One piece of shit at a time,” scaled up to the whole world.

Because for Yee, "shit" isn't just a swear word. It’s what the polished world is built on, the part of reality everyone helps create and no one wants to claim—the consequences, the leftovers, the mess that doesn’t vanish just because you refuse to see it. 

The newsletter treats modern life like a metabolism: every system takes in what it wants—food, money, attention, convenience—and puts something back out. Wastewater. Trash. Carbon. Bad data. Externalities with no owner. We love inputs because inputs feel like progress. Outputs feel like failure, or shame, or someone else's problem. So we build entire societies around pretending the output goes away.

Yee keeps dragging it back into view—not to scold, but to orient. Waste is honest: it tells you what a system really is, not what it claims to be. And his fix is the one he'd been using all along: don't drown in your output—close the loop.

Cleanup isn't a side quest. It's the plot.

Eighteen dispatches from the underside of modern life. That's what he left.

So, do I know Yee well?

No. I don't.

I didn’t know the full shape of his life. I didn’t know his private fears, his daily habits, the private machinery of his mind.

What I knew were scenes. Moments. Tiny glints of life—like a little bag of diamonds.

I know a laughing, youthful man who tried to get me to sprint in London.

I know a big, intimidating guy in a black shirt meeting my wife in a parking lot.

I know a father speaking about his new daughter with a tenderness that carried weight.

I know a writer who taught us that when the world feels like an endless pile of waste—digital, physical, or emotional—we don’t have to drown; we just have to be brave enough to deal with it the way he did, one piece of shit at a time, and in that spirit Yee’s closing reminder feels newly urgent: *The world is shitty enough out there, so let’s not be shitty to each other.*

And I know that’s enough to miss him.

So here’s what I’ll do with my small, incomplete knowledge of him: I’ll hold onto the parts I saw. I’ll laugh at the pushups. I’ll remember the parking lot. I’ll go back to the coffee shop where he turned his cup and quietly mapped a world where his daughter could breathe easier.

And I’ll try—like he kept trying—to be a little more useful when the shit hits.

Rest in peace, Yee.
